nameStory: The Spotted Tussock Moth gets its name from the distinctive tufts or 'tussocks' of hair that cover its caterpillar, combined with the black spots that often appear on the larva's yellow-orange middle section. The word 'tussock' originally described clumps of grass forming small hillocks, perfectly capturing the bumpy, tufted appearance of this fuzzy caterpillar.
description: The Spotted Tussock Moth is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1.5 inches across. While it belongs to the tiger moth family, it's commonly called a tussock moth because of its distinctively hairy caterpillar stage. The adult moths are active from late spring through mid-summer, while their eye-catching caterpillars can be found munching on tree leaves from summer into early fall.

idTips.label: Caterpillar appearance
idTips.description: The most recognizable stage - a dramatically fuzzy caterpillar with dense tufts of hair, black at both ends with a bright yellow or orange middle section that may have black spots

idTips.label: Wingspan size
idTips.description: Adult moths measure 35-45mm across (about 1.5 inches), making them medium-sized compared to other moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Flight timing
idTips.description: Adults are active from May through July, flying at night and often attracted to porch lights and windows

idTips.label: Caterpillar texture
idTips.description: The larva feels surprisingly soft and dense with its thick coat of hairs - like touching a bottle brush or small hairbrush

idTips.label: Host plants
idTips.description: Look for caterpillars feeding on leaves of common New England trees like maples, birches, oaks, willows, and basswood

habitat: Found throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests where their host trees grow abundantly. You'll spot the caterpillars on maples, birches, oaks, willows, poplars, alders, and basswood trees from lowland areas up into the mountains. They're particularly common in areas with diverse tree species rather than single-species stands.

seasonality.spring: Adult moths begin emerging in May, flying at night and mating. Look for them attracted to outdoor lights during warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak adult flight continues through July. Eggs hatch and tiny caterpillars begin feeding on tree leaves, growing through multiple stages.
seasonality.fall: Caterpillars reach their full size and most distinctive appearance in late summer and early fall before pupating. This is the best time to spot the iconic fuzzy larvae.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in cocoons hidden in bark crevices or leaf litter, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: Despite being called a 'tussock moth,' this species is actually a tiger moth that borrowed its common name from its caterpillar's appearance - it's like a tiger pretending to be a porcupine!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, the Hickory Tussock Moth caterpillar, but Spotted Tussock caterpillars have that distinctive yellow or orange middle section with black ends, while Hickory Tussock caterpillars are white with black spots throughout. Remember: 'Spotted' has a colorful middle, 'Hickory' is spotted all over.
contextualKnowledge: The naming can be confusing since this is technically a tiger moth (family Erebidae, tribe Arctiini) but everyone calls it a tussock moth because of the caterpillar's tufted appearance. True tussock moths belong to a different family entirely, showing how common names can sometimes blur scientific boundaries.
compareHints: The Spotted Tussock Moth differs from its closest relative, the Hickory Tussock Moth, primarily in the caterpillar stage - Spotted Tussock larvae have distinctive black ends with a yellow-orange middle, while Hickory Tussock larvae are predominantly white with black spots scattered across their entire body. Both species have similarly fuzzy, tufted caterpillars, but the color patterns make them quite distinguishable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Hickory Tussock Moth is distinguished from its close relative, the Spotted Tussock Moth, primarily by the caterpillar stage – Hickory Tussock caterpillars are pure white with black hair tufts, while Spotted Tussock caterpillars have distinctive yellow, orange, or red spots along their white bodies.
